title: Loops
description: for and while loops, range(), break/continue/pass, and the less common loop-else clause.
objectives: Write for loops over sequences and using range()
Write while loops and understand when to prefer each loop type
Use break, continue, and pass correctly

content.heading: for and while
content.body:
Python's for loop iterates directly over the elements of any iterable (a string, list, tuple, dict, range, file, etc.) — there is no traditional C-style for (init; condition; increment) form. To loop a fixed number of times, range(start, stop, step) generates a sequence of integers from start up to (but excluding) stop, stepping by step (default 1); range(5) is 0,1,2,3,4. while loops run as long as a condition stays true and are the right tool when the number of iterations isn't known in advance (e.g., reading input until the user types 'quit').

Nested loops (a loop inside another loop's body) are common for grid-like or combinatorial problems, such as printing a multiplication table.

content.heading: break, continue, pass, and loop else
content.body:
break immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop. continue skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one. pass is a no-op statement used as a placeholder where syntax requires a statement but you have nothing to do yet (an empty function body, for instance). A lesser-known feature: both for and while loops can have an else clause, which runs only if the loop completed normally — i.e., was never stopped by a break. This is useful for search patterns: 'loop through candidates; if none matched (no break happened), do X.'

A common beginner mistake is writing a while loop whose condition never becomes false because the loop forgets to update the variable being tested — producing an infinite loop.

content.explanation: The first loop stops early via break, so the else on it (if it had one) would not run. The second loop never breaks, so its else clause executes after the loop finishes normally.

keyPoints: for iterates directly over elements — range() generates integer sequences for counted loops
while is best when the number of iterations isn't known ahead of time
break exits the loop; continue skips to the next iteration; pass is a no-op placeholder
A loop's else clause runs only if the loop was never interrupted by break
commonMistakes: Forgetting to update the loop variable in a while loop, causing an infinite loop
Off-by-one errors with range()'s exclusive stop value
Assuming continue restarts the whole loop instead of just skipping to the next iteration
